title: Fire Wallet Gives AI Agents Separate Accounts for Limited Spending
summary: Fire Wallet Gives AI Agents Separate Accounts for Limited Spending
body_markdown:
[Fire Wallet](https://fire.co/) is building payments around a narrower question than whether an AI agent can buy something: how much money should that agent be able to reach? Its launch proposes a separate funded account for each agent, rather than giving software access to the owner's broader wallet.


The Fall 2026 Y Combinator company describes a pairing process using a QR code or link. The owner chooses an amount and a time limit, and the wallet creates an account with a key for that agent. Fire says the agent cannot see other accounts or spend beyond the balance assigned to it.


That turns delegation into an explicit allocation of funds. Instead of treating an agent as a person holding a general-purpose payment credential, Fire's model treats it as a separate spender with a bounded pool of money. An owner can top up that pool or revoke the account; according to the launch, revocation returns unspent funds to the owner's wallet.


[Watch Fire Wallet's original launch video](https://youtu.be/8raKMw5p1nU) .


Fire is targeting software that buys API access, data or compute, including purchases too small to fit comfortably into conventional payment workflows. The company says an agent can pay through an API call and quotes a transaction cost of a quarter of a cent regardless of the payment amount.


That price is a company claim, not a comparison established across every payment route. Its significance is the intended unit of commerce: an individual software action or small resource purchase, rather than a monthly subscription or a human-operated checkout. Whether that model is useful depends on providers accepting the payment method as well as agents being able to initiate it.


The launch also invites merchants to discuss checkout integrations. It does not provide a verified list of live merchants, payment volumes or customer deployments, so those ambitions should be kept separate from demonstrated adoption.


Fire describes the wallet as non-custodial and says payment amounts, senders and recipients are encrypted. It also advertises a unified view of payments across iPhone, Chrome and Mac. These statements describe the product as presented by its builders; the launch alone does not establish an independent security audit or guarantee anonymity.


The isolation of agent accounts addresses a different risk from transaction privacy. Keeping other balances outside an agent's reach can limit the funds exposed to that agent, while encryption concerns what observers can learn about payments. Neither, by itself, establishes that an agent will choose the right recipient or make a useful purchase.


Owners can also upload a Markdown file containing per-agent rules, according to Fire. The announcement does not explain the enforcement details of those rules, so they should not be confused with the explicit balance limit described in the account model.


YC lists Michael Divine, Joshua Goldbard and Manuel San Agustin as founders. The team points to experience building MobileCoin and private digital payments. Its new audience is agent developers and the businesses their software needs to pay. The immediate test is whether separate accounts, revocation and low-value transfers make delegated spending practical without requiring owners to surrender broad financial authority.
